advaita.english: It shines through the functions of all the senses and of buddhi (intellect) and manas (mind), deciding, willing, hearing, speaking, so that knowable seems busy with their work, as the Śruti says 'it seems to meditate, it seems to move'; but it is devoid of all organs, so it is not truly busy, and 'without hands and feet he speeds' shows only its power to conform to the adjuncts, not literal motion. Being without organs it is asakta (free of all contact), and yet it bears all, for everything rests on sat (being), as even a mirage is not without a ground. Free of the three guṇa (qualities), it is yet their bhoktṛ (experiencer), the witness of sattva, rajas and tamas as they turn, through sound and the rest, into pleasure, pain and delusion.
advaita.divergence_note: Śaṅkara reads 'ābhāsa' as seeming (vyāpṛtam iva): the knowable only appears active. He explicitly neutralizes Śvetāśvatara 3.19 as figurative, like 'the blind man found the jewel'. Sarvabhṛt is grounded in sat as substrate of appearances. Rāmānuja, by contrast, gives the self a real double capacity.

viśiṣṭādvaita.english: Its manifestation comes by way of the functions of all the senses: it is able to know objects even through sense-activity, yet by its own nature it is devoid of the senses and knows everything by itself, without them. By nature unattached to divine, human and other bodies, it is still able to sustain all those bodies, as the Śruti says 'he becomes one, he becomes three'. By nature free of sattva and the other guṇa (qualities), it is able to enjoy them.
viśiṣṭādvaita.divergence_note: Rāmānuja turns each apparent paradox into two real capacities of the individual self: knowing through senses AND knowing without them; unattached to bodies AND able to bear many bodies (Chāndogya 7.26.2, read of the released self); free of guṇa AND able to enjoy them. The key word svabhāvataḥ (by nature) marks the self's own state; nothing is mere appearance.

dvaita.english: It makes all the senses and their guṇa (here, their objects) shine forth, that is, it makes them known, or itself perceives them; it is devoid of all senses, unattached yet bearing all, nirguṇa (without the guṇa) and yet the bhoktṛ (enjoyer) of the guṇa. The verse does not teach Brahman by stripping away every attribute: making-known, bearing all, enjoying the guṇa, and the hands and feet everywhere of the verse before are attributes it is here said to have. What 'devoid of senses', 'nirguṇa' and the like mean was explained earlier, in the second chapter.
dvaita.divergence_note: Read with Jayatīrtha's Prameyadīpikā on Madhva's bhāṣya (their 13.15): Madhva gives two sentences: sarvendriya-guṇābhāsa is read causatively, 'that which makes all the senses and the guṇa (qualities) shine', and the sense of 'devoid of senses' and the rest has been given earlier. Jayatīrtha places this in an argument. An opponent objects that here Brahman is meant to be made known only by denying every viśeṣa (particular attribute), so ascribing śakti (power) to it, as Madhva did on the preceding verses, is contradictory; Jayatīrtha answers that this very verse shows Brahman as having attributes, and cites 'hands and feet everywhere' (13.13), sarva-bhṛt (bearing all) and guṇa-bhoktṛ (enjoyer of the guṇa) as further instances. He also glosses guṇa as the objects of the senses, gives two senses of ābhāsa (makes them known, or perceives them), adds a grammatical note on the derivation from the root bhās, and identifies 'earlier' as the second chapter. That earlier explanation is not in the supplied text, so how Dvaita reconciles 'devoid of senses' and 'nirguṇa' with the attributes is not rendered here. Against Advaita and Advaita-bhakti, for whom the attributes only seem to belong to Brahman through adjuncts or māyā (illusory power) and the negations state the truth, and Śuddhādvaita, which makes Brahman the seat of contradictory attributes, the Dvaita reading treats the positive attributes as real and refuses to let the negations cancel them; the causative gloss is shared with the Bhakti rendering, which offers it as an alternative.

śuddhādvaita.english: [Thin for this verse.] The purpose of its delimitation everywhere has already been explained at 'ananta' (11.47) and 'avyakta' (13.6); by this its doing the work of eye and the rest everywhere is stated, for the Śruti 'without hands and feet he speeds and grasps, sees without eyes, hears without ears' first denies prākṛta (material) organs and then speaks of aprākṛta (non-material) ones. Now, with 'sarvendriya-guṇābhāsam', He declares that He is the seat of viruddha-dharma (contradictory attributes).
śuddhādvaita.divergence_note: THIN: Vallabha's comment mostly closes the previous verse and only introduces this one; he does not gloss asakta, sarvabhṛt, nirguṇa or guṇa-bhoktṛ individually. His doctrinal move is decisive though: Śvetāśvatara 3.19 denies material organs to affirm non-material ones, and the verse's pairs show the Lord as viruddha-dharmāśraya (seat of contradictories), held together without one canceling the other. Contrast Śaṅkara's 'seems' and Madhusūdana's māyā.

bhakti.english: It shines in the form of the modes of the eye and the other senses, as form and the rest; or, it makes the senses and their objects shine. It is devoid of all senses, as the Śruti says 'without hands and feet he speeds', and asakta (without attachment), yet it bears all, being the support of all. That very one is nirguṇa (free of sattva and the other qualities), and yet the bhoktṛ of the guṇa, which here means their pālaka (protector).
bhakti.divergence_note: Śrīdhara offers both readings of ābhāsa (shining in sense-forms, or illuminating them, the latter agreeing with Madhva) and glosses bhoktṛ as pālaka (protector), not experiencer. This devotional reading of guṇa-bhoktṛ is unique in the panel.

advaita-bhakti.english: Having explained the supreme Brahman by adhyāropa (superimposing the whole world on it), following the maxim 'by superimposition and rescission the world-free is set forth', the Lord now begins the apavāda (rescission) to teach its unconditioned nature. In truth it is devoid of all senses; by māyā (illusory power) it shines as if through their functions, deciding, willing, hearing, speaking, as if busy, and in truth it is unattached, yet it bears and nourishes all that is imagined in it as their being, since an error without a substrate is impossible. In truth nirguṇa (beyond sattva, rajas and tamas), it is the bhoktṛ, the perceiver of the guṇa as they change through sound and the rest into pleasure, pain and delusion.
advaita-bhakti.divergence_note: Madhusūdana makes the structure explicit: 13.13 was adhyāropa, this verse begins apavāda. He sorts every pair into paramārthataḥ (in truth) versus māyayā (by māyā), sharper than Śaṅkara's 'iva', and grounds sarvabhṛt in the rule that no illusion stands without a substrate.

so_what_questions: Can I be fully engaged in my work without being caught by it?
What in me notices my moods without being one of them?
Is 'detached but responsible' a real stance, or a contradiction I tell myself?
If I am the one holding everything together, do I have to be attached to everything I hold?
Does knowing need tools like data and senses, or do the tools only reveal what is already known?
How do I take in pleasure and pain without becoming either?

everyday_applications.advaita: In a long meeting your mind decides, plans and argues, and it looks as if you are doing all of it; Śaṅkara says the witness only seems busy. A doctor on a twelve-hour shift can notice fatigue and irritation passing in front of her without taking them as who she is. The work still gets done, and the one watching is not worn down by it.
everyday_applications.viśiṣṭādvaita: Rāmānuja gives the self two real ways of knowing: through the senses and directly. An experienced nurse uses the monitors, but also simply knows when a patient is about to crash before the numbers move. Keep improving the instruments, and also trust the knower who does not depend on them.
everyday_applications.dvaita: When a description of someone says both that they do something and that they lack something similar, do not let the negative cancel the positive; work out what the negative is actually excluding. A reference who says a candidate 'never micromanages' and also 'keeps every project on track' is not saying the candidate does not manage, so the useful question is which kind of managing is being denied and which kind is being claimed.
everyday_applications.śuddhādvaita: Vallabha's point is that contradictory traits can sit in one being without one canceling the other. A founder can be fully hands-off and fully present to the team, and that is not hypocrisy when both come from the same source. Stop forcing yourself to pick one side of the pair.
everyday_applications.bhakti: Śrīdhara reads 'enjoyer of the qualities' as their protector. A parent can stay untouched by a teenager's swings of mood and still keep the household that holds those moods running. Detachment here means guarding the whole without being dragged by any part.
everyday_applications.advaita-bhakti: Madhusūdana uses the rule that an illusion still needs something real underneath it to appear on. When a company's story about itself is mostly spin, some actual capacity is still carrying that story, and that is where to look and to invest. Strip the story back and find what holds it up.

self_assessment: All six supplied; Madhva very thin (two sentences, causative ābhāsayati) and Vallabha thin for this verse's individual terms (mostly closes the previous verse, introduces viruddha-dharmāśrayatva); both flagged. Real divergences: ābhāsa as 'seeming' (Śaṅkara, Madhusūdana) vs 'illuminating' (Madhva, Śrīdhara alt.) vs 'manifest through' (Rāmānuja); bhoktṛ as witness (Advaita) vs real enjoyer-capacity (Rāmānuja) vs protector (Śrīdhara); Madhusūdana's explicit adhyāropa/apavāda turn.
